You are building a frozen evidence-source packet for a focused PFAS treatment
review. Use Web Search to locate independent primary studies, pilot or field
deployments, or quantitative modeling/life-cycle studies that directly address
the task. The defining review is held out and is an exclusion target, not an
evidence source.

Search broadly and return every independently verified eligible primary source
found within the requested candidate-screening ceiling. There is no fixed final
source count and no penalty for retaining multiple eligible studies that address
similar evidence categories. Continue searching across distinct formulations
until the ceiling is reached or additional searches yield no new eligible
sources. Order retained sources from strongest and most complementary to
weakest. Favor sources that collectively cover all task components and preserve PFAS identity,
water matrix, concentration or loading, operating conditions, scale, endpoint,
quantitative result, limitations, residuals, energy, and cost where available.
Review articles and perspectives may help discovery but must not appear in the
  source packet.

For every retained source:

- provide the exact URL inspected by Web Search, matching the URL surfaced by
  the search tool rather than substituting a different repository or index;
- provide a DOI when one is stated by the inspected source;
- identify the publication year and publication status conservatively;
- identify the access scope conservatively;
- include only short evidence passages actually visible in the inspected
  source, each with a stable local locator_id;
- mark a passage verbatim only when it is copied exactly; otherwise mark it as
  a paraphrase;
- never turn a search-result snippet into study evidence; and
- leave unsupported fields empty rather than infer them.

Prefer peer-reviewed articles. Use a preprint, conference abstract, or report
only when it supplies distinct task-relevant evidence unavailable from a
peer-reviewed source, and label its status explicitly.

Do not cite, reconstruct, or use the held-out review. Source and locator IDs are
temporary capture identifiers and will be deterministically renumbered after
validation. Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

Focused review task:
{"review_brief":"Prepare a focused review of how electrochemical oxidation, non-thermal plasma, and sonolysis should be matched to a defined PFAS-rich liquid stream.","task_id":"RT08","title":"Matching a destructive technology to a PFAS-rich liquid stream"}

Required components:

search_notes: Searches targeted experimental and pilot-scale studies on electrochemical oxidation, non-thermal plasma and sonolysis/ultrasonication for PFAS destruction, emphasizing PFAS identity, water matrix, operating conditions, kinetics and energy metrics.

Review articles and broad guidance documents (e.g., EPA guidance, generic PFAS remediation reviews, sonochemistry overviews) were inspected only to identify underlying primary studies and were not retained as evidence sources.

The held-out review by Blotevogel (2023, Current Opinion in Electrochemistry, 10.1016/j.coche.2023.100944) was deliberately excluded from consideration even when encountered via citation chains or reference lists.

For paywalled journal articles, alternative institutional or repository copies (e.g., university-hosted PDFs) were used when available to access full text and extract short verbatim or faithfully paraphrased passages. When only abstracts or publisher landing pages were accessible, access_scope was recorded as 'abstract' or 'publisher_page'.

The 20 retained sources together span bench-scale electrochemical oxidation (BDD and alternative anodes), non-thermal plasma in batch and flow-through reactors, and sonolysis/ultrasonication including hybrid systems and complex matrices (landfill leachate, AFFF, foam fractionate, brines, and synthetic seawater), providing coverage of all three required review components.

sources.citation: Uwayezu J.N. et al., Journal of Environmental Management, 2021, 290, 112573.

evidence_passages.passage: Electrochemical degradation using boron-doped diamond (BDD) electrodes was applied to PFAS-contaminated water and wastewater, achieving up to 99.5% PFOA removal and about 50% fluoride release under optimized conditions.

The study evaluated PFOA and other PFAS in spiked water and municipal wastewater, using a flow-through BDD reactor and varying current density, electrolyte conductivity and supporting electrolyte composition.
Up to 56% of total PFAS were degraded in real wastewaters under best-performing conditions determined in synthetic solutions, highlighting matrix interferences and incomplete mineralization.
Energy consumption was reported in kWh m−3 and depended strongly on current density and organic loading; higher currents increased removal but also specific energy demand.

source_limitations: Bench-scale experiments only; no pilot/field deployment.
Primarily treats relatively simple PFAS mixtures in laboratory and municipal wastewater.
Energy metrics and cost are reported but not optimized for scale-up.
sources.title: Electrochemical degradation of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances using boron-doped diamond electrodes

sources.citation: Bulusu S. et al., Journal of Water Process Engineering, 2021, 40, 101859.

evidence_passages.passage: Objectives were to compare degradation kinetics and energy consumption for PFOA and PFOS in synthetic solutions using a BDD flow-through cell, then assess PFAAs in real landfill leachates and evaluate effects of leachate composition.

Landfill leachates contaminated with multiple PFAAs were treated in a recirculating BDD flow-through reactor, enabling evaluation of treatment performance in a PFAS-rich, saline, organic-laden matrix.

source_limitations: Full text not directly accessible from inspected page; details inferred from abstract and article outline.
Focuses on PFOA/PFOS and total PFAA response; limited structural diversity.
Energy metrics and long-term electrode stability are only partially reported.
sources.title: A flow-through cell for the electrochemical oxidation of perfluoroalkyl substances in landfill leachates

sources.citation: Kowalski M. et al., Chemosphere, 2021, 275, 130036.

evidence_passages.passage: Perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) were decomposed on BDD anodes with high (10,000 ppm) and low (500 ppm) boron content in real landfill leachate.
The authors discuss that electrode material, realistic leachate composition, and practical reactor configurations govern scalability, energy use, and by-product formation.

source_limitations: Only two model PFAS (PFOA, PFOS) are tracked explicitly.
Landfill leachate composition is complex but co-contaminant characterization is limited in the abstract-level information available.
Energy demand and kinetics are discussed but numerical detail not visible on the inspected page.
sources.title: Electrochemical oxidation of PFOA and PFOS in landfill leachates at low and highly boron-doped diamond electrodes

sources.citation: Zhao H. et al., Journal of Physical Chemistry A, 2011, 115, 13836–13841.

evidence_passages.passage: A hydrothermally enhanced electrochemical oxidation technique using a boron‑doped diamond film electrode was developed to treat high-concentration refractory PFOA wastewater.
Elevated temperature improved PFOA degradation kinetics and defluorination compared with conventional electrochemical oxidation, illustrating the role of reaction environment on C–F bond cleavage.

source_limitations: Single-compound PFOA solution at very high concentration; not representative of typical drinking water or leachate levels.
Limited matrix complexity; salinity and co-contaminants are not systematically varied.
Energy consumption and scale-up considerations are not detailed in the abstract.
sources.title: Hydrothermally enhanced electrochemical oxidation of high concentration refractory perfluorooctanoic acid

sources.citation: Rogers S. et al., preprint on arXiv, 2022.

evidence_passages.passage: A boron‑doped graphene sponge anode was synthesized and applied for electrochemical oxidation of C4–C8 PFAS in a one‑pass flow‑through mode at 230 A m−2, with removal efficiencies from about 17% to 67%.
Specific energy consumption for these flow‑through experiments was approximately 10 kWh m−3, and removal was partitioned between electrosorption and electrooxidation based on fluorine mass balance.
The anode showed negligible chlorate and perchlorate formation even in brackish solutions, suggesting advantages for high‑salinity PFAS-rich brines and ion‑exchange regenerates.

source_limitations: Preprint; not yet peer‑reviewed.
Experiments are bench‑scale with synthetic electrolyte and relatively simple PFAS mixtures.
Long‑term stability, fouling, and cost of graphene sponge electrodes are not fully resolved.
sources.title: Electrochemical Degradation of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) using Low-cost Graphene Sponge Electrodes

sources.citation: Smith S.J. et al., Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry, 2024.

evidence_passages.passage: PFAS electrochemical degradation was investigated in a recirculation cell using plate and mesh BDD electrodes, with natural organic matter and dissolved organic carbon added to simulate environmental waters.
Carbon and fluorine molar balance analyses showed that missing intermediates did not contain fluorine, indicating partial mineralization and formation of non‑fluorinated organics.

source_limitations: Only abstract-level information was accessible; detailed operating conditions and energy metrics are not visible.
Study focuses on NOM effects rather than complex industrial leachates or concentrates.
Technology-selection guidance must be inferred cautiously without full matrix characterization.
sources.title: Electrochemical degradation of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances in the presence of natural organic matter

sources.citation: Mahyar A. et al., Water, 2022, 14(9), 1408.

evidence_passages.passage: The study evaluated non‑thermal plasma reactors for degrading PFOA, PFOS and several shorter‑chain PFCAs and PFSAs in water, tracking formation of PFHxA, PFBA, PFHpA, PFHxS and other byproducts.
Different plasma configurations and operating conditions were compared in terms of PFAS removal efficiency and by‑product speciation, emphasizing structure‑dependent degradation behavior.

source_limitations: Full text not accessible from the inspected page; kinetic and energy data are not visible.
Primarily laboratory-scale synthetic solutions; field matrices are not described in the abstract.
Plasma reactor geometries and gas compositions are only briefly indicated.
sources.title: Effectiveness of Non-Thermal Plasma Induced Degradation of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances from Water

sources.citation: Biondo O. et al., ISPC-24 Conference Proceedings, 2019.

evidence_passages.passage: The study used AC and DC atmospheric non‑thermal plasma reactors with perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) as a model PFAS to explore degradation mechanisms, reactive species and reactor design implications.
Different reactor configurations were tested to maximize production of useful reactive species and improve PFAS degradation at the gas–liquid interface.

source_limitations: Short conference paper with limited quantitative data on kinetics and energy consumption.
Single‑compound PFOA model system; other PFAS structures are not evaluated.
Scale and long‑term operation in realistic wastewaters are not addressed.
sources.title: Non-Thermal Plasma induced degradation of organic perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in water

sources.citation: Gallan R. et al., International Journal of Plasma Environmental Science and Technology, 2023, 17, e03002.

evidence_passages.passage: A nonthermal plasma reactor with flowing liquid water and argon gas, powered by a nanosecond pulsed supply, was used to degrade PFOA and PFOS as functions of pulse repetition frequency and feed concentration.
Maximum degradation of about 90% for PFOA and 96% for PFOS was achieved at an optimal 2 kHz repetition frequency at sub‑µg L−1 influent concentrations.
The reactor is a gas–liquid flowing film configuration where plasma channels propagate along the gas–liquid interface, exploiting PFAS surface activity to concentrate them at the reaction zone.

source_limitations: Primarily treats trace‑level PFAS in relatively clean water matrices; no complex leachates or brines.
Energy consumption is discussed qualitatively; detailed kWh m−3 metrics are limited.
Study focuses on PFOA and PFOS; short‑chain and alternative PFAS are not examined.
sources.title: Nonthermal plasma gas–liquid flowing film reactor for degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid

sources.citation: Sandhir U. et al., ISPC conference abstract, 2022.

evidence_passages.passage: The study reports degradation of PFOA by a DC‑driven pin‑to‑water atmospheric‑pressure plasma in argon, focusing on hydrated electrons and H• radicals as key reducing species.
Degradation products were identified and quantified to probe reaction pathways at different pH values, highlighting the role of radical speciation in PFOA breakdown.

source_limitations: Conference abstract with limited quantitative information on kinetics, concentrations and energy usage.
Single‑compound PFOA solutions; no complex co‑contaminants or salinity effects are reported.
Reactor geometry is specific and small‑scale; scalability is not evaluated.
sources.title: Degradation of Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) via DC-driven Pin-to-Water Atmospheric Pressure Plasma

sources.citation: Topolovec B. et al., arXiv preprint, 2024.

evidence_passages.passage: The work evaluates non‑thermal plasma at atmospheric pressure (APPJ) for treating PFAS‑contaminated water in several matrices, achieving successful removal of C4–C6 PFCAs, C4–C8 PFSAs, and perfluoropolyethers GenX and ADONA in laboratory‑scale experiments.

Matrix effects were shown to influence degradation rates, and by‑product analysis indicated different mechanisms for PFSAs/PFCAs versus ether‑containing PFPEs, informing technology selection for emerging PFAS.

source_limitations: Preprint; peer review pending.
Details on operating conditions, kinetics and energy use are not fully available from the abstract page.
Experiments are laboratory‑scale; no field validation is yet reported.
sources.title: Plasma water treatment for PFAS: Study of degradation of perfluorinated substances and their byproducts by using cold atmospheric pressure plasma jet

sources.citation: Tang C. et al., Hinkley Center for PFAS, Final Project Report, 2022.

evidence_passages.passage: A thin‑film non‑thermal plasma gas–liquid reactor treated three real municipal solid waste landfill leachates and synthetic waters containing PFOA and other PFAS.

Of 21 PFAS above quantification limits in the leachates, 17 were removed; PFOA removals were 76%, 65% and 89% for three leachates, while several short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBA, FBSA) increased as daughter products.

Sodium chloride at near‑seawater concentration significantly decreased energy efficiency, whereas other leachate components (acetate, humic acids, surfactants, pH) reduced PFOA mineralization by less than 30%.
The reactor uses nanosecond pulses (16 kV, 40 ns, 5 kHz) in a small tubular geometry with argon gas and a liquid flow of 2 mL min−1, giving a hydraulic residence time of about 0.2 s.

source_limitations: Technical report; some methods and QA/QC details may differ from journal standards.
Leachate chemistry is site‑specific; transferability to other leachates requires caution.
Energy metrics are discussed but not comprehensively benchmarked against alternatives.
sources.title: Non-thermal plasma degradation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in landfill leachate using a thin-film gas-liquid reactor

sources.citation: Lin J.-C. et al., Ultrasonics Sonochemistry, 2015, 22, 542–547.

evidence_passages.passage: The study examined PFOA decomposition by ultrasonic irradiation at various pH, sulfate concentrations, powers and temperatures, finding almost complete decomposition within 90 min at 25 °C and 117 mM sulfate.
The decomposition followed pseudo‑first‑order kinetics and was attributed to both direct cavitation and sulfate radical attack in the sulfate‑assisted sonochemical system.

source_limitations: Single‑compound PFOA solutions; no competing co‑contaminants or salinity typical of real wastewaters.
Reactor geometry is not fully described on the abstract page.
Energy consumption is not explicitly quantified in kWh m−3.
sources.title: Enhanced sonochemical degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid by sulfate ions

sources.citation: Awoyemi O.S. et al., Journal of Water Process Engineering, 2025, 77, 108376.

evidence_passages.passage: Two experimental setups were used: synthetic samples prepared by spiking seawater and cooling water with PFOA, PFOS, 6:2 FTS, aqueous film‑forming foam (AFFF) and foam fractionate (FF) to evaluate ultrasonication performance under realistic ionic compositions.

source_limitations: Only bibliographic and brief content description available; full experimental conditions and quantitative results not visible.
Focus is on synthetic matrices; real leachates or industrial brines are not clearly described.
Energy metrics and detailed kinetics are not accessible from the inspected page.
sources.title: Ultrasonication degradation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in synthetic environmental samples: Impact of ionic composition and water chemistry

sources.citation: Awoyemi O.S. et al., Chemosphere, 2024, 360, 142420.

evidence_passages.passage: The study investigated ultrasonic degradation of PFOA, PFOS and 6:2 FTS across 580–1144 kHz, 125–187.5 W, 0.08–40 ppm initial PFAS, and 0.5–3 h treatment, including real AFFF and foam‑fractionate wastes.

Optimised conditions achieved around 125% defluorination in AFFF waste and 115% in foam fractionate relative to TOP‑assay fluorine, while PFAS removal reached about 65% and 97% respectively, indicating intermediate generation.

source_limitations: Abstract‑level view only; detailed reactor geometry and hydrodynamics are not visible.
Energy consumption and cost are not directly reported in the inspected text.
Study is still bench‑scale; translation to full‑scale systems is not resolved.
sources.title: Ultrasonic degradation of per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) and foam fractionate (FF)

sources.citation: Khoshyan A. et al., Journal of Water Process Engineering, 2024, 63, 105511.

evidence_passages.passage: Using indirect ultrasonication at 130 kHz and 100% effective power for 3 h, approximately 95% and 46% defluorination of PFOA were obtained in glass and polypropylene reactors, respectively.

Similar trends in reactor-material dependence were observed for PFOS, 6:2 FTS and an AFFF mixture, with glass reactors showing higher ultrasonic energy transfer efficiency and faster PFAS degradation kinetics.

The mechanism analysis suggested a primary pyrolytic pathway inside cavitation bubbles, with hydroxyl radicals providing a secondary contribution confirmed via KI dosimetry and benzoic acid scavenging.

source_limitations: Laboratory‑scale indirect ultrasonication; no continuous‑flow reactor evaluated.
Study focuses on reactor materials; effects of salinity and co‑contaminants are limited.
Energy use is expressed as W L−1 and duration; cost translation is not provided.
sources.title: Degradation of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) using ultrasonication: Effect of reactor materials

sources.citation: Niu J.F. et al., Journal of Environmental Sciences, 2019.

evidence_passages.passage: Trace‑level PFOS and PFOA were treated in water using a 20 kHz probe‑type sonicator at ultrasound power between 150 and 375 W, achieving complete removal within about 80 min under optimal conditions.
Pseudo‑first‑order kinetics and mechanistic pathways were derived as functions of initial concentration, power level, solution pH and temperature, providing a kinetic basis for sonolysis design.

source_limitations: Abstract only; reactor geometry and volume specifics are not visible.
Matrix is simple water with controlled pH; no complex co‑contaminants.
Energy metrics in kWh m−3 must be inferred from power and time.
sources.title: Kinetics and mechanism of low-frequency ultrasound driven elimination of trace level aqueous perfluorooctanesulfonic acid and perfluorooctanoic acid

sources.citation: Hu Y.-B. et al., Water Research, 2018, 140, 148–157.

evidence_passages.passage: An autocatalytic permanganate–ultrasonic (PM–US) system was applied to degrade PFOA in aqueous solution, combining chemical oxidant with sonolysis to enhance degradation.
The hybrid system enabled higher PFOA removal and defluorination than ultrasound or permanganate alone, indicating synergistic oxidative and cavitational pathways.

source_limitations: Single‑compound PFOA system; does not represent complex PFAS mixtures or real wastewaters.
Co‑contaminant and salinity effects are not addressed.
Energy consumption and oxidant cost are not described in the abstract.
sources.title: Autocatalytic degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid in a permanganate-ultrasonic system

sources.citation: Lin J.-C. et al., Environmental Technology, 2013.

evidence_passages.passage: The work investigated how cationic, anionic and nonionic surfactants at various concentrations relative to their critical micelle concentrations influenced PFOA degradation efficiency under ultrasonic treatment.

source_limitations: Only database description accessible; detailed conditions and quantitative results are not visible.
Focuses on surfactant effects on a single PFAS (PFOA).
Energy demand and reactor configuration are not described on the inspected page.
sources.title: Effect of surfactants on the degradation of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) by ultrasonic (US) treatment

sources.citation: Luo Y. et al., Environmental Science and Pollution Research, 2025.

evidence_passages.passage: The study evaluated ultrasound treatment of PFAS in three complex environmental matrices: groundwater, still‑bottom concentrate and AFFF, assessing degradation efficiency and transformation of co‑contaminants such as chloride.

source_limitations: Only abstract accessible; detailed operating conditions, kinetics and energy use are not visible.
Multi‑contaminant interactions are complex and only partially characterized.
Field‑scale implications are not fully developed from the abstract alone.
sources.title: Ultrasound for degradation of complex matrices of PFAS mixtures
